newsitem.title: USA: Massive turnover in key U.S. land, water plan.
newsitem.headline: Massive turnover in key U.S. land, water plan.

text.p: The nation's biggest soil and water conservation programme will enroll 16 million acres this fall and deliver more environmental benefits at lower cost, Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Thursday.
It would be the largest turnover of land in the Conservation Reserve, which pays farmers to idle fragile land for 10 years, since it was created in 1985.
In total, the farmland to be placed in the reserve is about the size of West Virginia.
"This is probably the most important environmental programme in government," Glickman told a news conference, because it involves private land.

The reserve's aims are to reduce erosion, protect water quality and improve wildlife habitat. In its early days, the reserve was aimed as much at constraining farm output as conservation, but those days are gone, Glickman said.
"A higher (acreage) number at this time would have retired more productive land and a lower number would have missed out on some tremendous conservation opportunities," he said.
American Farmland Trust, a land preservation group, said the new focus for the reserve "is a significant step toward realising the enormous conservation potential of this programme."

Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman Richard Lugar, Indiana Republican, applauded the "more environmentally targeted and economical" reserve and cautioned the government against idling so much land that food production suffered.

Because enrollment would be smaller than the expiring acrege, about 5 million acres would be freed for crops and livestock. Farmers will be given another chance this fall to offer land for the reserve.

Sen. Pat Roberts, who played a leading role last year in retooling the programme, and House Agriculture Committee Chairman Bob Smith said the Clinton adminstration broke faith with farmers by accepting too little land.
"This is a completely inadequate effort on the administration's part," said Smith, Oregon Republican.
Roberts, a Kansas Republican, said Glickman should order enrollment of "the remaining 6 million authorised CRP acres as quickly as possible."
Annual rent on the new land will average $39 an acre, down from $50 at present.
Agriculture Department officials said about 1 million to 1.5 million acres of land planted with corn, wheat and soybeans would return to production, a fairly nominal amount.
The Plains states and the Corn Belt would continue to dominate the Conservation Reserve under the new enrollment.

North Dakota would become the top state for Conservation Reserve enrollment with a total of 3.35 million acres, including 2 million accepted this fall. Texas, now the largest state, probably would drop to No. 2.

Enrollment fell in the upper Midwest. Minnesota would drop from 1.56 million to 791,824 acres. Iowa, with 1.74 million acres, would drop to 1.29 million acres. Michigan and Wisconsin each would decline by about 100,000 acres.
